Organization Background

Olist: Brazil’s B2C Marketplace

A decentralised marketplace — thousands of independent sellers, one platform. Olist doesn’t sell anything itself; it facilitates listings and logistics support. Sellers list products, customers browse and buy and review, and Olist earns a commission on every transaction.

The structural risk

Sellers manage their own inventory and shipping independently — Olist has no direct control over stock or packaging quality. So one seller’s mistake still shows up as “Olist’s fault” to the customer. That single fact shapes almost everything below: demand, delivery, and loyalty all run through partners the platform can influence but not command.

The Analyst’s Brief

Three Questions Keeping Olist Up at Night

Brought in to turn transaction data into decisions, treating demand, delivery, and customer value as three unknowns worth quantifying.

01

Unpredictable Demand

Order volume swings month to month, with a sharp spike every November that current planning doesn’t anticipate — sellers get no advance signal before stock runs out right when it matters most.

Objective: quantify the seasonal pattern and growth rate.
02

Delivery Delays

~6.8% of delivered orders arrive late, and satisfaction drops sharply once they do. Is it distance, seller location, order size, or timing? No prior analysis isolates the driver.

Objective: model delay to find what actually drives it.
03

No Segmentation

Every customer is treated the same in marketing, regardless of value or loyalty — high-value and one-time buyers are currently indistinguishable in the business’s own data.

Objective: build data-driven segments for targeted retention.
Data & Method

Nine Tables, Four Methods, One Honest Pipeline

The Olist Brazilian E-Commerce dataset (Kaggle) was the only source large enough to cover a full order lifecycle — purchase through delivery through review — in one coherent set: orders, order items, payments, reviews, customers, sellers, products, a category translation table, and geolocation. Everything else was smaller, synthetic, or missing the timestamps and reviews this brief needed.

01 Exploratory analysis — Tukey’s principle, explore before modelling 02 Time-series trend — linear fit quantifies growth rate 03 RFM + K-Means (k=4) — z-score standardised, elbow-validated 04 Multiple regression — signed, interpretable delay drivers

Cleaning before counting

Missing delivery timestamps are structural — the order simply never arrived — so they were excluded, never imputed. Payments were regrouped from 103,886 instalment rows to one row per order, and customer identity was deduplicated for the segmentation work.

Fig. — Missing values by column

Every gap is a delivery that never happened, not a data-entry slip.

Fig. — Dataset size through the pipeline

99,441 orders in, 96,470 clean rows out — a 3% trim, not a rewrite.

The difference it made

Imputing missing delivery dates would have fabricated ~2,965 outcomes. Excluding them instead keeps every delay figure in this story 100% real.

What Sells, When, and How People Pay

The first read of the data: steady growth through 2017–18 with a spike no calendar warns you about, a Monday-heavy ordering rhythm, revenue concentrated in a handful of categories, and one payment method carrying nearly three-quarters of all volume.

Steady growth through 2017–18, with a sharp November (Black Friday) spike.

Fig. 2 — Orders by day of week

Monday is busiest at ~16,196 orders, tapering steadily to the weekend.

Health & Beauty leads; the top 10 categories account for ~63% of revenue.

Fig. 4 — Payment methods

Credit card is 73.9% of volume — the cheapest, largest campaign audience on the platform.

Result 2 of 4 · The Headline Finding

Delivery Timing Is the Single Biggest Lever on Happiness

4.31 → 1.73
Average review score, very-early delivery vs. very-late — a near-monotonic drop. No other variable in the dataset moves satisfaction this much.
Fig. 5 — Review score by delivery timing

Score falls almost in a straight line as deliveries run later.

Fig. 6 — Distribution of delivery delay

93.2% of deliveries arrive early, by an average of 13.51 days; the 6.8% that are late overrun by 10.62 days on average.

Fig. 7 — Growth trend

+307 orders/month, with average order value rising from BRL 120 to 185 over the window — growth compounding on itself.

Key takeaways
  • Delivery timing is the single biggest lever on customer happiness — this answers Objective 2 directly.
  • Delivery-window recalibration is the highest-leverage recommendation in this project.
  • The November demand spike is predictable — sellers can be given eight weeks’ notice.

What it means
  • Losing 10% of High-Value Champions is a real, measurable revenue hit — not a rounding error.
  • Loyal Customers (2,772) prove repeat purchase is achievable on this platform — it’s just rare.
  • Segmentation directly answers Objective 3: value and loyalty are now visible, not assumed.
Result 4 of 4

What Actually Drives a Late Delivery

A regression against order, timing, and geography features turned up three surprises — and one honest limit.

+2.02 days

Seller based in São Paulo

Hub congestion beats geography — the most central shipping point is also the most jammed.

+1.93 days

Seller & customer, same state

Also a routing artifact, not a distance effect — proximity doesn’t guarantee a faster route.

−0.58 days

Each extra item in the order

Multi-item orders are batched and shipped faster, not slower.

Fig. 11 — Regression coefficients

Red bars increase delay, blue bars reduce it.

Fig. 12 — Actual vs. predicted delay

The model captures direction, not magnitude — the honest limitation below explains why.

Stated, not hidden

R² = 0.026. This secondary dataset has no carrier-level routing data — which is very likely where the real explanatory power lives. The direction of every effect above is still reliable; the size of the effect is a floor, not a ceiling.

Interpretation & Recommendations

Quantified Actions, Honest Limits

Four moves, each sized against the data above rather than a hunch — with the conversion assumption stated plainly next to the number.

01

Recalibrate delivery windows & decongest the São Paulo hub

Target late-rate 6.8% → 4.0–4.5%
~2,434 orders shifted from late to on-time
Effect
−2.3 pts late rate
02

14-day re-engagement campaign, targeted at credit-card users

50,642 New/Recent customers × 8% conversion
Reaches the 73.9% of buyers already on the cheapest payment channel to campaign against
Projected impact
≈ BRL 652,230
03

VIP programme for High-Value Champions

2,418 customers × 10% churn risk × BRL 1,161 avg. spend
Protects the segment spending ~7× the platform average per order
Revenue protected
BRL 280,708
04

8-week seller advance notice before the November spike

37,526 Dormant customers × 5% win-back
Turns a predictable demand spike into a stocked, staffed one
Projected impact
≈ BRL 302,066
Limitations

Where This Analysis Stops

  • No carrier-level routing data — R² capped at 0.026 on the delay model.
  • The study window (Sep 2016–Oct 2018) predates post-pandemic e-commerce shifts.
  • product_weight_g existed in the raw data but couldn’t be reliably joined at the order level.
  • The high one-time-buyer rate may partly reflect how the dataset itself was constructed.
Conclusion

Delivery timing is the lever. One-time buyers are the growth.

São Paulo hub congestion is measurable and addressable. The next step is an ARIMA/Prophet forecast layered on carrier-level routing data — the piece this secondary dataset couldn’t provide.
